history.heading: Ancient Armenia
paragraphs: The Armenian Highlands have been inhabited since prehistoric times; the world's oldest known leather shoe and one of the oldest wineries were found in Armenian caves. The kingdom of Urartu flourished there in the 9th to 6th centuries BCE, and Yerevan traces its origins to the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BCE.
An Armenian kingdom emerged after the conquests of Alexander the Great. Under Tigranes the Great in the 1st century BCE it briefly became an empire stretching from the Caspian to the Mediterranean.

history.heading: First Christian nation
paragraphs: Armenia became the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion, traditionally dated to 301 CE. Around 405, the monk Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet, which is still used today.

Over the following centuries Armenia was repeatedly divided and ruled by larger empires: Rome and Persia, Byzantium and the Arab caliphates, and later the Seljuks, Mongols, Ottomans and Persians. A medieval Armenian kingdom also existed in Cilicia, on the Mediterranean coast, until 1375.

history.heading: Genocide and Soviet rule
paragraphs: In the 19th century eastern Armenia came under Russian rule, while western Armenia remained Ottoman. During the First World War, the Ottoman government carried out the Armenian Genocide of 1915–1923, in which around 1 million or more Armenians were killed and most survivors were deported or fled, creating a global diaspora.

A short-lived independent republic existed from 1918 to 1920 before Armenia became part of the Soviet Union. In 1988 a devastating earthquake struck the north, and the same year a conflict began over Nagorno-Karabakh, an Armenian-populated region within Soviet Azerbaijan.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Armenia became independent in 1991. War with Azerbaijan ended in 1994 with Armenian forces controlling Nagorno-Karabakh and surrounding districts. The Velvet Revolution of 2018 brought peaceful political change.

Azerbaijan regained much of the territory in a 2020 war and took full control of Nagorno-Karabakh in a 2023 offensive, after which nearly the entire Armenian population of the region, over 100,000 people, fled to Armenia. In 2025 the two countries agreed on the text of a peace treaty.

culture.heading: Language and faith
paragraphs: Armenian forms its own branch of the Indo-European language family and is written in its unique alphabet. The Armenian Apostolic Church is central to national identity, and Armenia is home to some of the oldest churches in the world, such as Etchmiadzin Cathedral.
A large diaspora, living mainly in Russia, the United States and France, is larger than the population of Armenia itself and plays an important role in culture and the economy.

culture.heading: Arts and traditions
paragraphs: Medieval Armenian monasteries such as Geghard and Haghpat are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and khachkars, carved stone crosses, are a distinctive art form. The duduk, a woodwind instrument made of apricot wood, gives Armenian music its characteristic mournful sound.
Famous people of Armenian descent include the composer Aram Khachaturian, the singer Charles Aznavour and the painter Arshile Gorky. Chess is extremely popular and is taught in schools.

culture.heading: Food
paragraphs: Lavash, a thin flatbread, is recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage. Other dishes include khorovats (barbecue), dolma, harissa porridge and apricots, a national symbol. Armenian brandy is world famous.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Since constitutional reforms took effect in 2018, Armenia has been a parliamentary republic in which the prime minister holds executive power and the president has a largely ceremonial role. The National Assembly is elected by proportional representation.
Since the 2018 Velvet Revolution, politics has been led by Nikol Pashinyan's Civil Contract party, with the defeats in Nagorno-Karabakh being a central political issue.

politics.heading: Shifting alliances
paragraphs: Armenia has long relied on Russia for security and is a member of the Eurasian Economic Union. Disappointed with Russia's role during the conflicts with Azerbaijan, it froze its participation in the Russian-led CSTO military alliance and has moved closer to the European Union and the United States.
Normalising relations with Azerbaijan and Türkiye, whose borders with Armenia have long been closed, is a major priority, as is international recognition of the Armenian Genocide.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Armenia is a landlocked country with limited natural resources, apart from copper, molybdenum and gold, which are important exports. Agriculture, brandy and wine, and food processing are significant.
The information technology sector has grown strongly, and Yerevan has become a regional tech hub. Remittances from Armenians working abroad, especially in Russia, are an important source of income.

economy.heading: Recent trends
paragraphs: The economy grew rapidly after 2022 as Russians and Russian businesses relocated to Armenia and trade flows were rerouted. Closed borders with Azerbaijan and Türkiye limit trade, with routes running through Georgia and Iran. The currency is the dram.
